idiom_name: std::variant<OrderPlaced, OrderCancelled> + std::visit with an overload set
implementation_notes: The modern C++ default for a closed event set: each event is a plain struct (identifiers plus a std::chrono time point), the set is a std::variant alias, and dispatch is std::visit over an overload set or a generic lambda with if constexpr. The variant replaces the abstract event base class and the visitor replaces the handler registry for reactions known at compile time; when handlers must be registered at runtime, key a std::function map on a type tag on top and accept the type-erasure cost.
pitfalls: std::visit requires the visitor to be callable for every alternative; a missing overload fails with a wall of template diagnostics, so keep the event set small and the overload set in one place.
A variant list is a closed set: adding an event type recompiles every visitor - the opposite of the runtime registration a classic registry gives you.

variants.name: Polymorphic event hierarchy + visitor / type-keyed dispatcher (classic)
variants.idiom_name: abstract DomainEvent base + accept(visitor) / std::map<type key, handler list>
variants.implementation_notes: The GoF-era realization: every event is a class deriving from an abstract DomainEvent with a virtual destructor, an occurred-on accessor and an accept() method; reactions are either Visitor implementations or a registry of handler lists keyed by a type tag. Choose it when the event set is open (plugins, modules), when events must be polymorphic values in heterogeneous containers, or when the codebase predates C++17.
pitfalls: Keying dispatch on typeid/type_index misses subclasses unless you walk base types, so a derived event silently reaches nobody.
Handlers stored as std::function in a long-lived registry outlive the objects they capture; unregistration and ownership need an explicit owner.

variants.name: Boost.Signals2 signals and slots
variants.implementation_notes: When the reactions are really a subscription list, Boost.Signals2 supplies the publisher: one boost::signals2::signal per event type, slots connected with automatic connection tracking, and thread-safe emission. The event structs stay plain data and the signal is the bus. Prefer it over a hand-written registry when connection lifetime, disconnection order and thread safety are the hard parts; keep it out of the domain layer if the model should stay free of Boost types.
pitfalls: A slot that outlives the object it captures crashes on the next emission; use scoped_connection or track the connection explicitly.
Emission is synchronous and serialized by the signal's mutex, so a blocking slot stalls every publisher thread.
